passage: Looking back, I, Wasim, can see how fast it spread. It started as a quarrel between Rehana and Tushar about who owned the vendor project. Within two weeks the lunch table had split: Rehana's side by the window, Tushar's by the fridge. Someone made a chat group without Tushar in it, then another without Rehana. I was in both, and said different things in each. Shameful, honestly. Devika, our manager, clearly felt something was off. She asked in a meeting, 'Is everything okay with the team?' Nobody said a word. So the guesses started: that Rehana wanted Devika's job, that Tushar was leaving, that Devika played favourites. None of it was true. The one true thing, the project quarrel, nobody ever told her.

qa.q: Where did Rehana's side sit at the lunch table?
qa.a: Rehana's side sat by the window.

qa.q: Why does Wasim now call being in both chat groups 'shameful'?
qa.a: Looking back, he feels guilty for saying different things to each side and feeding the split instead of calming it.

qa.q: What could have stopped the rumours from multiplying?
qa.a: If someone had told Devika the real cause, the quarrel over project ownership, she could have dealt with it directly instead of everyone guessing.

qa.q: What was it like for Devika to sense tension but hear nothing when she asked?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and anxious, left to guess while rumours even pulled her own fairness into question.

grounding: A colleague looks back on how a two-person quarrel split the team through lunch seating and chat groups while the manager, never told the cause, faced rumours.

passage:
Manager's note, Elizabeth, Friday.
Something is wrong on the design team and I can't see what. Three signs this week. The Thursday lunch table, which used to be one long noisy row, has split in two. When I walked into the kitchen, Anjali and two others stopped talking. And a junior told me, awkwardly, that there's 'a group chat drama', then refused to say more.
I've now heard three different theories: that Anjali is being pushed out, that I favour the senior designers, that someone complained to HR. None came from the people actually involved.
What I did: asked each team member for fifteen minutes one-to-one next week, with one open question, 'What's making work harder right now?' No names needed. I want the cause, not the rumours.

qa.q: What happened when Elizabeth walked into the kitchen?
qa.a: Anjali and two others stopped talking.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth seem to feel about the three theories?
qa.a: Unsettled and wary; the note suggests frustration that guesses are spreading while the real cause stays hidden.

qa.q: Why is Elizabeth's plan of one-to-one talks a sensible step?
qa.a: Private, open questions without needing names make it safer for people to share the actual cause, so Elizabeth can act on facts instead of rumours.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel on hearing the rumour about being pushed out?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel anxious and hurt, and might pull further into one side of the split.

grounding: A manager notes a team splitting at lunch and in chat groups, senses tension without knowing the cause, and hears multiplying rumours.

passage:
Diary, Thursday
The office is officially split. At lunch, Preeti's table was whispering about Karan "sabotaging" the launch. At the chai counter, Karan's friends were saying Preeti steals credit. I sat with neither group and ate my paratha standing up.
Then the chat group. Someone made a new one without Preeti in it. I left it after an hour. Felt sick reading it.
Our manager called me in today and asked, "Amandeep, what's going on with the team? Everyone's so tense." I said, "Just deadline stress, I think." Why did I say that? Because I didn't want to be the one who told. Now she's guessing, and the guesses are worse than the truth.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep eat lunch?
qa.a: Standing up, with neither group.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep feel sick reading the new chat group?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uncomfortable and uneasy, seeing colleagues ganging up and not wanting to be part of it.

qa.q: What small step could Amandeep take now?
qa.a: Go back to the manager and describe the actual disagreement between Preeti and Karan, without taking sides, so guesses stop multiplying.

qa.q: What is the manager experiencing as she senses the tension?
qa.a: She is likely worried and confused, feeling the strain but not knowing its real cause.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching others take sides in lunch talk and chat groups while the manager senses tension but is not told the cause.

passage:
The district health office in Sitapur shared one long room, so Leela heard everything. By Wednesday, the three field officers ate lunch apart from the two data clerks. Someone had said the clerks had blamed the field team for the missed report. Someone else said a clerk was being moved.
Leela didn't believe half of it. But she noticed Seema, their manager, pausing at the doorway after lunch, looking from one table to the other.
"Leela, is something going on?" Seema asked her by the water cooler.
Leela thought of the missed report, the real start of all this. "You should ask them both together," she said finally.

qa.q: Where was the district health office?
qa.a: In Sitapur.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling as she thought of the missed report?
qa.a: Leela seemed torn and uneasy, not wanting to gossip but worried the rumours were growing.

qa.q: Why was Leela's answer to Seema a helpful choice?
qa.a: It pointed the manager to the real cause and to both sides together, instead of adding another rumour.

qa.q: What is Seema experiencing as she pauses at the doorway?
qa.a: Seema senses tension and feels concerned and confused, noticing the split tables without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching staff split into sides over rumours while the manager senses tension but lacks the real cause.

passage: In the small architecture office in Aarhus, Ulla noticed the lunch table first. For years the whole team had crowded around one long table with rye bread and coffee. This week it had split: three people at the window end, four near the kitchen, and Ines in between, eating fast, her eyes on her plate. When Ulla walked into the drawing room, a laugh stopped halfway. On Wednesday she saw two phones light up at the same moment during a meeting, and two people exchanged a look. Someone mentioned "the group chat" and went quiet. Ulla asked Ines, casually, whether the competition entry was going all right. "Fine, all fine," Ines said, not looking up. By Friday Ulla had heard three different explanations in the corridor, and none from anyone willing to say it to her face.

qa.q: How had the lunch table changed this week?
qa.a: It had split: three people at the window end, four near the kitchen, and Ines in between.

qa.q: What might Ulla be worried about by Friday?
qa.a: She is uneasy and worried that the team is dividing and rumours are spreading while nobody tells her the real cause.

qa.q: What could Ulla try next?
qa.a: She could talk privately with people one at a time about what is getting in the way of the work, rather than relying on corridor explanations.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines, sitting between the two groups?
qa.a: Ines seems caught in the middle, eating fast and avoiding eye contact, perhaps under pressure to pick a side.

grounding: Shows colleagues taking sides at lunch and in a group chat while the manager senses the tension but hears only guesses, never the cause.
